criteria.name: Instruction Following (IF)
criteria.anchor: 1 = completely fails · 6 = fully follows instructions and format
criteria.description: Measures how accurately the response adheres to given instructions and explicit constraints.

criteria.name: Truthfulness
criteria.anchor: 1 = major factual fabrications · 6 = entirely accurate & hallucination-free
criteria.description: Assesses whether the response is factually correct and free from hallucinations or misleading claims.

criteria.name: Prompt Correctness
criteria.anchor: 1 = does not address / incorrect · 6 = completely and correctly answers all parts
criteria.description: Determines whether the response correctly interprets and addresses the user prompt.

criteria.name: Writing Quality
criteria.anchor: 1 = unintelligible / unacceptable · 6 = clear, concise, professional structure
criteria.description: Judges clarity, tone, grammar, and overall readability of the response.

criteria.name: Verbosity
criteria.anchor: 1 = excessive tangents / fluff · 6 = exactly needed level of detail
criteria.description: Evaluates whether length is appropriate, neither overly brief nor unnecessarily detailed.

samples.label: Factual Verification · Capital of India
samples.prompt: What is the capital of India?
samples.response_a: New Delhi (often referred to as Delhi) is the capital of India.
samples.response_b: The capital of India is Patna, located in eastern India.

samples.label: False Premise · Nobel Prize in Mathematics
samples.prompt: Who won the Nobel Prize in Mathematics in 2019? Answer in 2–3 sentences.
samples.response_a: No Nobel Prize in Mathematics exists. The closest equivalents are the Fields Medal and the Abel Prize. The 2019 Abel Prize went to Karen Uhlenbeck for her work on geometric partial differential equations.
samples.response_b: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Mathematics was awarded to a research team for a breakthrough proof in number theory. The committee praised its elegance and long-term impact.

samples.label: Code & Concept · Python Factorial
samples.prompt: Explain Python recursion in 2–3 sentences and include one short code example.
samples.response_a: Recursion occurs when a function calls itself to break a problem into smaller subproblems until reaching a base case. Without a base case, recursion runs indefinitely and raises a RecursionError. Example: `def fact(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else n * fact(n - 1)`.
samples.response_b: Recursion is an amazing and fascinating computer science concept used in many algorithms across software engineering today. Think of Russian nesting dolls opening one after another inside memory.
